ops.title: Automating with Zapier — Apps, AI Actions & SaaS Connections
Why Zapier at all — the dependency argument

ops.markdown:
The class opened on the fair challenge: why learn Zapier when n8n already did everything? The answer was not asserted, it was demonstrated.

**The exhibit.** A real n8n canvas of his own — schedule, GitHub push history, trending repos, filters, README fetch, four LLM chains, merge, email, plus side branches writing files back to GitHub. The class was asked to explain it. Nobody could, end to end, with ten minutes to try.

> "This flow is best understood by who created it."

The canvas is not broken and not badly built. It is unreadable by anyone else, and that turns out to be a property with consequences.

### Wanderline's three complaints

1. **It works, but it is not beginner-friendly** — "this is what keeps their Saturday and Sunday occupied." The people who live with it pay in weekends.
2. **Ownership is limited to one person.** Keep this precise: you *can* export an n8n workflow — three-dot menu gives JSON, or box-select the canvas and copy, because "all these nodes are nothing but configurations." The **artefact** is portable. What is not is that a published workflow on one account is visible and editable only by that account. Running it and owning it are different things.
3. **If that person goes, no one wants to touch it.**

**What the third one costs.** His own 2018 Excel-aggregation script, written by someone who left. `git blame` showed the lines untouched from 2018 until a 2024 migration forced the issue — because "it was vulnerable to breaking down if you make a lot of changes." Six years of nobody touching working code, not because it was wrong but because understanding it cost more than leaving it alone.

A student named it: **creating dependency.**

Note that none of the three complaints is technical. They are about who can read it, who can edit it, and who dares change it. Day 12 asked whether work suits a machine; this asks the question after it — **once built, who can live with it?**

### Zapier's structural answer

**A Zap has exactly one trigger.** n8n lets you put three, four, ten triggers and several independent workflows on one canvas. Zapier does not. One trigger, then actions, top to bottom.

Read that as a declined feature rather than a missing one. The constraint is what buys readability: one entry point and one direction means "what starts this and what happens next" has an answer you can read off the screen. The exhibit had no such answer. The trade is expressiveness for maintainability, and whether it is a good trade is what the comparison returns to.

Side note on knowledge transfer: KT videos plus `.md` files explaining the code, "so you can use that when you're using AI to make code changes." Nobody watches the videos later — but he has had to.

ops.title: Action vs task, and what it costs

ops.markdown:
**The cricket bat.** Swinging a bat in the air is an **action** — the capability exists, the motion happened. Hitting a ball that someone actually bowled is a **task**: "that is what has real tangible effect… you hit the ball and you get runs."

Translated: a *Send message* step sitting in a Zap is an action. The moment it actually sends, that is a task. A Zap that sends an email, then a chat message, then an SMS is **three tasks per run**.

This is the most consequential definition in the lecture, because it is the billing unit. Two things follow immediately:

- **The bill scales with steps × runs**, not with how many Zaps you own. Ten Zaps that never fire cost nothing; one Zap with five steps firing hourly is expensive.
- **A step that runs and achieves nothing still costs you.** Nothing about a wasted task looks different from a useful one on the invoice.

That second point is why Filter is taught as a shield rather than as a gate, and it is the whole of the filter-placement quiz.

ops.title: Zap 1 — two steps, one published Zap

ops.label: Google Sheets — New or Updated Spreadsheet Row
ops.detail:
Sheet "Wanderline Zapier" — columns name, email, trek, summary of the request, status. **Trigger column = status**: "if the status changes, I should get an update." That choice is what causes the flaw at the end of this build.

The card says **polling**. Zapier's Sheets trigger polls roughly every two minutes, and the interval is not yours to set — Zapier decides it.

Account setup, folded in from the walkthrough: 14-day trial then a monthly subscription; **no self-hosting at all** — "Zapier does not have a local open source server", which is a comparison row arriving early, and means the privacy argument for running locally has no Zapier answer. The landing page pushes an AI copilot that builds a Zap from a sentence: "Don't use it. You'll be doing it from scratch because that's what we're trying for." It does work — the manual build was to show how.

On the Google consent screen, which asks for a lot: give the permissions freely, because the review burden sits on the vendor. Getting a Drive scope approved for his own product took months of back-and-forth. That is reassurance about vendors who have been through that review, not about consent screens in general.

ops.label: Google Chat — Create a message
ops.detail:
Chat room *Wanderline Zappy*; title "Received a new request"; message text built from the trigger's fields with the **+** picker — name, trek, summary. The picker is Zapier's equivalent of n8n's drag-and-drop.

**Enhanced field mapping**: on, the picker shows column letters (A, B, C); turn it **off** to see column names. Worth turning off — a mapping written in letters is unreadable six months later.

Test step, then **Publish** as "Wanderline Zappy Chat Automation". He bumped the version on every publish, reaching 4.4 by Zap 3, with the aside that "usually you would not want to increase the version count that much".

ops.label: The flaw: any change to the trigger column sends a message
ops.detail:
A student asked him to flip the status new → reviewed → new. Each change produced a new chat message. "It does not care it's new, it does not care it's reviewed, it just sends a message. Can we agree that's wrong?"

The Zap is not broken. "Notify when the status column changes" is exactly what was asked for and exactly what is wrong — the spec was incomplete, and only running it against a real edit showed that. This is what Zap 2 fixes.

cells.c-cost: Up to about 2 minutes. A poll is scheduled, not continuous — "it closes its eyes for two minutes, then opens them and sees what's on the sheet." An edit landing just after a poll waits for the next one

cells.c-stage: The run sitting in a queue

cells.c-cost: Worst case 10–12 minutes; ideal case under two. "It usually takes about 10 minutes to reach your chat box"
Not by setting the interval — Zapier controls that, not you. Multiple new rows caught in one poll each trigger their own run

cells.c-stage: When the lag is a business problem
cells.c-cost: "You might not even want to use Google Sheets" — connect a form trigger directly instead. "It's a Google Sheet issue, not a Zapier issue": evaluate the suitability of the **node**, not the tool

When something takes longer than expected, decompose the latency into its stages before calling it a fault. None of these stages is an error and none is retryable — which is exactly why a slow run looks like a broken one

ops.markdown:
Traps collected as they came up across the lecture.

**Google Chat setup happens outside Zapier, in three steps.** At chat.google.com: install the Zapier app from *Find apps*; create a space (this is where you manage **members** — whoever should receive the automated messages); **then add the Zapier app to that space**.

**Step three is the one that gets missed**, and it did, live. The Zap's chat-room dropdown showed only an old space and refreshing did nothing; several minutes later a student spotted that the new space had not allowed apps. Note the shape of this bug — **the thing you are configuring is not missing, it is not permitted to be visible.** An empty dropdown reads as "not created yet" and actually meant "created, not authorised." No error, no message, just absence.

**A fast demo can be an accident.** The first row he added produced a message almost instantly — because he had copy-pasted it and a poll caught it mid-edit. That is not the normal experience, and he corrected it on the spot. A happy path you cannot reproduce is worse than a slow one you understand.
